reason: The text depicts King David abusing his governmental authority for personal sinful purposes—seducing Bathsheba and orchestrating Uriah's death in battle to cover his sin. The passage explicitly states 'וַיֵּרַע הַדָּבָר אֲשֶׁר־ עָשָׂה דָוִד בְּעֵינֵי יְהוָה' (the thing David did displeased the Lord). Nathan the prophet's confrontation condemns these acts as violations of God's covenant, and God pronounces judgment including the death of David's child and bloodshed in his household. Rather than modeling good leadership benefiting the people, this passage exemplifies the abuse of governmental power for personal gain and the violation of justice—the opposite of ethical leadership.
